content.title: A clearer picture of training intensity

blocks.text: Two thresholds divide this fictional cyclist's power into three zones. Below LT1 is Zone 1; between LT1 and LT2 is Zone 2; above LT2 is Zone 3. Move the power slider to see where the example falls.
The numbers are teaching inputs, not a test result. Changing a threshold changes this example; it does not show how a real athlete adapts.

assumptions: All threshold values in this lesson are fictional teaching inputs.
The display includes exact thresholds in Zone 2 and labels them separately; this is a UI convention.
The cited study used ventilatory thresholds; it does not validate these example lactate-threshold values.

lessonTypes.name: Three training zones
lessonTypes.description: Explore supplied, fictional LT1 and LT2 boundaries using cycling power.

sources.title: Quantifying training intensity distribution in elite endurance athletes: is there evidence for an optimal distribution?
sources.authors: Stephen Seiler and Glenn Øvrevik Kjerland
sources.supports: A three-zone framework delineated by two ventilatory thresholds in the studied athletes.
sources.limitations: This study used ventilatory thresholds. It does not validate this example's LT1/LT2 wattages, a lactate-threshold algorithm, or equivalence between ventilatory and lactate thresholds.

claims.text: The display assigns Z1 below the first supplied boundary, Z2 from the first through the second boundary, and Z3 above the second boundary. Exact boundaries are labelled separately.
All power thresholds are fictional teaching inputs. Editing them changes the example and does not estimate an athlete's thresholds or predict adaptation.
Seiler and Kjerland used two ventilatory thresholds to delineate three intensity zones in their study of endurance athletes.

evidenceSnapshot.notice: The current lesson uses fictional power boundaries. Source notes describe the scope of the research; every authored lesson remains a draft until the creator reviews it.
